subject: Architecture
title: Biomimicry in Design
description: A micro-lesson that makes Biomimicry in Design usable.

hook.text: Termite mounds maintain 87°F inside while outside temperatures swing from 35°F to 104°F — without electricity.

buildup.text: Architects studied this — the Eastgate Centre in Zimbabwe copies termite ventilation and uses 90% less energy.

discovery.text: Biomimicry copies nature's solutions — lotus leaves inspire self-cleaning surfaces, spider silk inspires cables.

twist.text: Shark skin patterns are being applied to building surfaces — they reduce drag and resist bacterial growth.

climax.text: After 3.8 billion years of evolution, nature has already solved most engineering problems. We just need to copy.

punchline.text: The best architect on Earth isn't human. It's evolution.

quiz.question: What natural model inspired the Eastgate Centre's ventilation?

details.summary: Biomimicry applies strategies found in nature to architectural design — termite mounds inspire passive ventilation, lotus leaves inform self-cleaning surfaces, and bone structures guide material optimization. Nature has refined solutions over millions of years of evolution.
details.whyItMatters: Nature has solved every engineering problem architecture faces — ventilation, structure, waterproofing, thermal regulation. Biomimicry taps this vast library of tested solutions, often producing designs that outperform conventional engineering.
takeaways: Biomimicry applies biological strategies to building design
Termite mounds, bones, and leaves inspire architectural solutions
Nature's solutions have been refined by millions of years of evolution

faq.question: What is the best-known biomimicry building?
faq.answer: The Eastgate Centre in Harare, Zimbabwe, modeled its ventilation on termite mounds. Passive airflow through the building maintains comfortable temperatures without air conditioning, using 90% less energy than comparable conventional buildings in the same climate.

faq.question: How do architects learn from nature?
faq.answer: Through cross-disciplinary collaboration with biologists who identify natural strategies matching architectural challenges. The Biomimicry Institute facilitates these connections. Architects also study structures like spider webs, bird skulls, and coral reefs for structural inspiration.
